lead: Older buses such as ARINC 429 are slow one-way links. A modern aircraft needs dozens of computers to exchange large blocks of data with a guaranteed delay. AFDX — Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet, standardised as ARINC 664 part 7 — meets this with 100 Mbit/s switched Ethernet plus virtual links that reserve bandwidth. Fibre-optic cable carries data as light, giving high bandwidth, low weight and no pickup of electrical interference. Both appear in airliner avionics bays and in fly-by-light research.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.7 for how a data bus defines words, timing and error checks.

sections.h3: Why a switched network replaced bundles of wires

blocks.text: ARINC 429 is a one-way link: one transmitter, up to twenty receivers, 100 kbit/s. An airliner has dozens of computers that must exchange large blocks of data. Wiring each pair separately needs hundreds of cables and adds weight. AFDX replaces the bundle with a switched network.

AFDX means Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet; the standard is ARINC 664 part 7. Every link runs at 100 Mbit/s in both directions at once. Two kinds of equipment sit on the network. An end system is the AFDX interface inside one avionics computer: it builds frames for its host, sends them, and delivers frames addressed to it. A switch reads the destination of each frame and forwards it only to the port that leads to the receiver.

Each link is full duplex and point-to-point, so there are no collisions. A port never hears another port's traffic while it transmits. Heavy traffic between two computers does not slow a third pair, provided the reserved bandwidths fit on each link. The price is that the whole traffic pattern must be defined before flight and loaded as a configuration table.

The same ARINC 664 part 7 network is used on large Airbus and Boeing types to carry flight control, display and maintenance data. Office Ethernet cannot promise a delay; AFDX can, and that is why aviation adopted it.

sections.h3: Virtual links, BAG and redundancy management

blocks.text: A virtual link (VL) is a one-way logical path from one source end system to one or more destination end systems. A 16-bit VL ID in each frame identifies it. Frames of many VLs share the same physical switches, but each VL has capacity reserved for it in advance.

Two numbers define a VL. BAG, the bandwidth allocation gap, is the minimum time between the first bits of two consecutive frames of that VL. Allowed values are powers of two from 1 ms to 128 ms. Lmax is the largest frame, in bytes, that the VL may send. From these two numbers the reserved bandwidth follows.

blocks.where: Lmax is the maximum frame size of the VL in bytes; the 8 converts bytes to bits; BAG is the bandwidth allocation gap in seconds; the result is in bit/s. The source paces itself to send at most one frame of size Lmax per BAG.

blocks.text: Switches reserve that share on every link the VL crosses, so the worst-case delay of a frame can be computed before the aircraft flies. Certification needs exactly that: a bound, not an average.

Redundancy management: each end system normally connects to two independent networks, A and B, with separate switches and wiring. Every frame is sent on both. Each frame carries a sequence number from 0 to 255 that counts per VL. The receiver checks the Ethernet CRC and the sequence number, keeps the first valid copy, and discards the duplicate or any out-of-order frame. One failed switch or one cut cable costs nothing.

A fibre-optic link turns electrical data into light, carries the light in glass, and turns it back. Three parts: a light source driven by the transmitter circuit, the fibre, and a detector that converts light back into current.

The source is an LED or a laser diode. The fibre is a glass core inside a cladding of lower refractive index. Light in the core that strikes the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection: it reflects back into the core instead of escaping, so it stays guided along the fibre. The detector is a PIN photodiode, or an avalanche photodiode where more sensitivity is needed.

Two kinds of fibre. Multimode fibre has a wide core, about 50 or 62.5 µm, and carries many light paths; it is cheap and suits short runs inside the aircraft, commonly at 850 nm. Single-mode fibre has a core near 9 µm and one path; with a laser at 1300 or 1550 nm it reaches far with low loss.

items: Advantage — bandwidth: Gbit/s on one strand.
Advantage — weight: one fibre replaces a bundle of copper cables, and weight costs fuel.
Advantage — immunity to EMI: the signal is light and the fibre is dielectric, so there is no conduction, no ground loop and no spark risk near a fuel tank.
Disadvantage — connectors must be polished and cleaned; a dirty connector loses more signal than a kilometre of fibre.
Disadvantage — tight bends leak light, so a minimum bend radius is specified.
Disadvantage — connectors, splices and test sets cost more, and a fibre cannot deliver power to a remote sensor.

blocks.text: Aircraft that signal flight control surfaces over fibre are called fly-by-light; see Flight Control Systems.

examples.question: A camera sends images over one AFDX virtual link. Its configuration table entry gives BAG = 2 ms and Lmax = 1000 bytes. (a) Find the reserved bandwidth in bit/s and in Mbit/s. (b) Find the maximum number of frames per second the link may carry.
steps: Convert the frame size to bits: 1000 bytes × 8 = 8000 bits.
Convert the BAG to seconds: 2 ms ÷ 1000 = 0.002 s.
Reserved bandwidth = 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG = 8000 bits ÷ 0.002 s = 4 000 000 bit/s.
Frame rate limit = 1 ÷ BAG = 1 ÷ 0.002 s = 500 frames per second.
Check: 500 frames/s × 8000 bits = 4 000 000 bit/s, which matches step 3.
examples.answer: The virtual link reserves 4 000 000 bit/s, that is 4 Mbit/s, and may carry at most 500 frames per second.
examples.check:
lmax_bytes = 1000
bag_ms = 2
bits = lmax_bytes * 8
rate_bps = bits * 1000 / bag_ms
mbps = rate_bps / 1e6
frames_per_s = 1000 / bag_ms
print(bits)
print(rate_bps)
print(mbps)
print(frames_per_s)

traps: AFDX is not office Ethernet: no CSMA/CD, no random access. Every link is full duplex and switched, and the traffic pattern is fixed in a configuration table before flight.

Unit slips in 8 × Lmax ÷ BAG: Lmax is in bytes, so multiply by 8; BAG is listed in milliseconds, so divide by 1000. Writing BAG as 2 instead of 0.002 s makes the answer 1000 times too small (4000 bit/s instead of 4 000 000 bit/s).
BAG is the minimum spacing between two frames of one VL. It is not the frame transmission time and not the maximum end-to-end latency.
Fibre removes electrical interference, not the need for redundancy. Switches, connectors and fibres still fail, so networks A and B both stay.
Lmax is a maximum, not an average. Reserved bandwidth must cover the worst case, so always use Lmax.

quiz.q: What does the bandwidth allocation gap (BAG) of a virtual link define, and what values may it take?
quiz.a: The minimum time between the first bits of two consecutive frames of that virtual link. Allowed values are powers of two from 1 ms to 128 ms.

quiz.q: Name the light source, the medium and the detector in a fibre-optic link.
quiz.a: Source: LED or laser diode. Medium: glass fibre with core and cladding. Detector: PIN photodiode or avalanche photodiode.

quiz.q: Why does an AFDX network have no collisions, when older shared Ethernet did?
quiz.a: Every link is a full-duplex point-to-point connection into a switch. A station transmits on one pair and receives on another, and the switch buffers and forwards frames, so two stations never share one transmission medium.

quiz.q: AFDX uses ordinary Ethernet frames. Why can its delay still be guaranteed?
quiz.a: Each VL has a fixed Lmax and BAG in a configuration table, and switches reserve that rate on every link it crosses. Worst-case queueing delay is therefore computable before flight, unlike best-effort office Ethernet.

quiz.q: A virtual link has BAG = 8 ms and Lmax = 1500 bytes. Find its reserved bandwidth.
How long does one 1500-byte frame occupy a 100 Mbit/s AFDX link?
quiz.a: 1500 × 8 = 12 000 bits. 12 000 ÷ 100 000 000 = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ s = 120 µs. 120 µs is for the payload bits only; headers, preamble and interframe gap add a few more microseconds.

quiz.q: An engineer argues: 'We use fibre everywhere, so the second AFDX network can be removed.' Give two reasons why this is wrong.
quiz.a: Fibre removes electrical interference and ground loops, but it does not stop broken fibres, dirty or loose connectors, failed switches or switch power loss; redundancy covers those failures, not only EMI. Also, certification of a single-channel design would need a quantified failure rate showing the loss of the network is extremely improbable, which a single path cannot demonstrate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Deterministic Ethernet has spread well past aviation: the ideas inside ARINC 664 part 7 reappear in IEEE 802.1 time-sensitive networking, now used in cars and factory control. Researchers work on gigabit AFDX and on optical backbones with optical switches inside the aircraft. Fly-by-light, where even flight control signalling is optical, has flown in demonstrators but not in service airliners. Search next for 'ARINC 664 part 7', 'AFDX virtual link BAG', 'time-sensitive networking' and 'fly-by-light'.
